analysis.one_liner: Makes failed bank executives repay up to five years of pay and shifts losses to holding-company investors.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote in the Senate Banking Committee despite bipartisan sponsorship and three hearings, and it died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: After a bank fails and the FDIC steps in, this bill would require the FDIC to take back up to five years of compensation—salary, bonuses, stock-based pay, and stock-trading profits—from executives responsible for the failure. The recovered money would go into the federal deposit insurance fund or the Treasury. It would also make the creditors and shareholders of a failed bank's parent company absorb the bank's losses, rather than leaving them with the deposit insurance system.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers and bank depositors benefit because recovery money would flow into the Deposit Insurance Fund, the fund that backs Americans' bank accounts. The clawback also aims to deter executives from chasing short-term bonuses with risky bets, since they would personally pay if the bet fails. Soundly run banks benefit too, because executives at failing banks would no longer keep the upside while the insurance fund absorbs the downside.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Deposit insurance fund and bank customers

how_it_helps.text: The FDIC would be required to claw back all or part of five years of compensation—salary, bonuses, incentive pay, equity awards, and stock-trading profits—from any executive responsible for a failed bank's condition, to prevent unjust enrichment and make the executive bear losses in proportion to their responsibility [S2] [S3].
Clawed-back money would be deposited into the Deposit Insurance Fund or the Treasury, replenishing the fund that protects ordinary depositors [S3].

The bill would require that the creditors and shareholders of a failed bank's holding company bear the bank's losses, keeping those losses off the deposit insurance system that backs ordinary bank accounts [S2] [S3].
It would also expand the FDIC's clawback authority over parties responsible for losses at large financial companies, regardless of which legal process put the FDIC in charge [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Executives of failed banks would repay up to five years of pay. Creditors and shareholders of the failed bank's parent company would absorb losses they might otherwise have escaped, which could also raise their cost of funding bank holding companies.
analysis.who_pays_short: Failed bank executives and parent-company investors

drawbacks.text: A five-year clawback reaching back before any failure is a broad penalty; executives and their lawyers would likely contest it, and the FDIC would face litigation and hard choices about who was 'responsible' for a failure [S3].

Banks could respond by restructuring executive pay upfront—higher fixed salaries, fewer incentive bonuses—which would raise banks' fixed costs without necessarily changing risk-taking, and the rule only bites after a bank has already failed, too late to protect depositors in that instance.
Making holding-company creditors and shareholders bear losses could make it somewhat more expensive for bank holding companies to raise money, a cost that could be passed on in loan pricing.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit—executives who run a bank into the ground do not keep five years of pay while the federal deposit insurance fund absorbs the damage—directly addresses a problem highlighted by the 2023 bank failures. The administrative and litigation burden on the FDIC is real but manageable, and the effect on overall credit costs is modest. The bill does nothing to prevent a failure before it happens, so it is a backstop rather than a full fix.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Senate Banking Committee, which held hearings on bank failures but never voted on the bill, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 29, 2023, in the weeks after the Silicon Valley Bank and Signature Bank failures, and was referred to the Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee [S1] [S5].

It had bipartisan support from the start: Elizabeth Warren introduced it with Republican senators Josh Hawley and Mike Braun and Democrat Catherine Cortez Masto, and it drew four cosponsors split evenly between the parties [S3] [S4].
The Banking Committee held three hearings in May 2023—printing one as S.Hrg. 118-441—but the record shows no markup, no vote, and no floor action for the rest of the Congress [S5].
The bill died in committee when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Executives of failed banks keep their compensation, and holding-company creditors and shareholders are not required to absorb their banks' losses. The Deposit Insurance Fund, which ultimately backstops ordinary depositors, gains nothing from the recoveries the bill would have produced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Failed bank executives and holding-company investors

for.name: Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Failed Bank Executives Clawback Act and gathered bipartisan cosponsors.

for.name: Josh Hawley
for.what_they_did: Original cosponsor, giving the bill Republican support from day one.

against.name: Sherrod Brown
against.role: Chair, Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee that referred the bill to and held hearings on bank failures in May 2023 but never brought the bill to a committee vote.

sides.party_line_note: Support was evenly bipartisan at introduction—Warren (D) with Hawley and Braun (R) as original cosponsors, plus Cortez Masto (D), for a 2-2 bipartisan cosponsor list—but the committee where Democrats held the majority never voted on it.

industries.note: The bill would make them repay up to five years of salary, bonuses, equity awards, and stock-trading profits when their bank fails under FDIC receivership. Their interest in keeping that pay runs against depositors and the insurance fund that protects them.
The bill writes into law that they, not the deposit insurance system, bear the losses of a failed bank. Today that allocation is a policy choice; the bill would remove the chance of rescue.

Most banks would never fail, so the direct cost falls only on executives and investors at failed banks. Banks with sound management would face less competition from institutions that pay executives for risky short-term gains, though holding companies could face somewhat higher funding costs.
The FDIC would receive clawed-back compensation for the fund that backs ordinary Americans' bank accounts, reducing pressure on the fund and on any premiums other banks pay to replenish it.
